thread.title: Amarin Plays Out, CBL Assets Get A Closer Look - The Idea Guide

author: The Idea Guide
title: Amarin Plays Out, CBL Assets Get A Closer Look - The Idea Guide
text:
by Daniel Shvartsman
Checking Seeking Alpha and Twitter ( TWTR ) last night after a dinner (Spanish time) was a fairly immersive experience. Between the ongoing rehashing of yesterday's confirmation hearings in Congress for Brett Kavanaugh and, closer to home, the news of the SEC filing suit against Elon Musk, it was hard to lift my head from the iPad for a bit.
I'm going to set aside the political story, but even with the Musk story there's in theory some value in following the headlines. These stories can be illustrative of key market themes, they can focus attention on major trends to watch, and in this case they can also be entertaining. But I find them frustrating as a source of investing content. One of the tensions at Seeking Alpha or anywhere in the financial media is that attention is paid to a story like this even though the unearthing of alpha is much harder.
On the Idea Guide I try to find a balance of hot stories that may have some actionable takeaways and under the radar stories that may be more rewarding to review and consider as a jumping point for due diligence. Because while it sometimes seems like the site revolves around 5-10 stocks, there's a lot more going on.
We have a good selection this week, with one battleground playing out somewhat decisively and a couple ideas related to spin-offs that could be worth checking out. On the short side, an author with a solid track record takes a look at another battleground stock, while steel looks like it is about to bend if not break.
Long Ideas We published 283 long ideas in the past week. Tech continues to hold readers' attention, with BABA, AAPL, QCOM, and MU among the stocks generating most page views this week. Here are a few articles that are a little off the beaten path, the first one aside.
Amarin 'Proves It' by DoctoRx I reviewed an Amarin ( AMRN ) article two weeks ago in the run-up to the release of key results from the company's Reduce-It trial. I didn't have much to say beyond presenting the short idea, but I tend to be bearish about biotech companies going into trials as a base rate. And that tendency would have played out wrong with Amarin!
In light of the company's stunning market rise, DoctoRx reviews the results of the trial. Making the key caveat that the released results so far are just the headline numbers, he says there is indeed reason to be excited and that this could import significant revenue growth. The crux of the story is, "between net price increases, a large and well-defined new indication, and geographic expansion, a 10X increase in sales is a mid-case scenario. No guarantees, and we - and the FDA - have to see all the data, of course."
I've written about how a successful trial and approval is not victory in and of itself, and there are still fish oil alternatives out there. But the company already has some scale with $200M in sales, which is much easier to build on than starting from zero, I would think.
Sentiment Check - There is excitement but not quite euphoria - skeptics pop up in the comment streams to remind that this is still just fish oil reformulated. And our articles - four have been published since the trial - all make the point about the likelihood of a share offering to shore up AMRN's balance sheet, and a couple point out that the data is still pending.
Double Your Money In Valvoline By Betting Against Disruption by Atlas Research This idea on Valvoline ( VVV ) has a lot of big market themes implicated in it. For example, Atlas Research focuses on the threat to Valvoline's brand based on Amazon's ( AMZN ) private motor oil - Amazon eating the world and the declining power of brands are both common themes. Then there is consolidation in various industries - Atlas Research argues VVV can just buy up smaller peers, while Jiffy Lube is swamped by being part of Royal Shell ( RDS.A ) and not as nimble as a result. And something that does not get addressed here at all - how much is motor oil levered to the auto cycle in general? Or (since that feels like a weaker argument to me) how much is motor oil threatened by changes to the way we will drive over the next 10-15 years?
My sense is not very much, at least in the interim years. Which makes this an interesting opportunity to explore.
Sentiment Check - Valvoline has been a bit under the radar since it spun off from Ashland ( ASH ) in 2016, but the coverage we've had has been bullish. The comment stream briefly raises the threat of electric cars, and has a long discussion on the sustainability and pricing of VVV's high returns on invested capital.
Why We Believe Henry Schein's Upcoming Animal Health Spin-Off Will Unlock 30% To 50% Upside by Ben Axler File in the 'notable when a short seller goes long' category. Ben Axler of Spruce Point Capital shares a long idea on Henry Schien's ( HSIC ) pending spin-off of its animal health business. I just did a month of spin-off reviews for the Idea Guide and missed this one, apparently because it will be filing an S-1 and an S-4 (as the animal health business is going to be combined with Vets First Choice, a private company). So I guess it's good we can get it into the Idea Guide one way or another.
The story seems to be more about the quality of Vets First Choice as a business, which would make it even further removed from investors' radar. The company has been around since 2010 and is founded and led by Benjamin Shaw. Shaw is the son of David Shaw, who founded IDEXX ( IDXX ) and who is the chairman of the board for VFC. There are a few parts to this transaction, which may add complexity and obscure the value. The multiple Axler is using to value the eventual VFC is healthy - 25x 2020 EBITDA - but it may be a little early to slap multiples on anyway, given we don't know how this will price. It is an interesting story.
Sentiment Check - This is the first article we've had on HSIC focused on the spin-off. The comments suggest concerns over HSIC's legacy dental business, which may be long in the tooth in this cycle.
Lilis Energy: Lots Of Leverage Here And Potential Profits by Long Player Leverage is a thing that cuts both ways. I bring up an example where the leverage may be too much in the short ideas below. Long Player makes the case that Lilis Energy ( LLEX ) is the flip side, where the oil & gas producer has bet big on key acreage in the Permian basin. "Either this company goes bust in one of the bigger squishes of the year or the company becomes a very large home run from the higher oil pricing combined with the financial leverage." We're at that point in the oil cycle where big swings may be rewarded by market participants and there still may be enough time to take the swing before the bottom falls out. So this may be a timely case to consider.
Sentiment Check - Long Player is the only one covering this stock, and has been bullish with the stock remaining rangebound. Commentary is mostly bullish, though some question the acreage valuations Long Player throws out.
Preferred Bank Not Getting The Preference It Deserves by Long Term Investor I've mentioned before that I'm a sucker for articles about small banks trading out of line with their value. Long Term Investor offers Preferred Bank ( PFBC ) as an option. The company posts impressive numbers - net interest margin over 4%, efficiency ratio around 35%, and return on equity of nearly 19% - and yet the stock trades at 13x earnings, is slightly down over the last 12 months, and has lagged the sector as a whole. What gives? The author essentially assumes it's market irrationality. I can add at the surface level that the company is trading for 2.36x tangible book value, and that the company's loan book is primarily real estate and then commercial. I'm not sure that gets an answer, but interesting to look at.
Sentiment Check - What is out there is positive - we have one article from earlier this year and one article per year, more or less, prior to that.
Short Ideas We published 16 short ideas in the past week. Tesla ( TSLA ) makes up five of them, and this is before the news broke about the SEC suing Elon Musk. Tilray ( TLRY ) continues to draw smoke with two short ideas, though that story may be burning out. As ever, we have a few interesting ideas, including a classic Seeking Alpha battleground.
CBL & Associates: Is The Stock Worth $0? by Michael Boyd One of the early Idea Guides I wrote was a look at Omega Healthcare ( OHI ), a high-yielding healthcare REIT that has attracted a lot of opinions on Seeking Alpha on both sides of the trade. It was inspired in part by the prevalence of stories like this on Seeking Alpha, where a high-yielding REIT or other yield co attracts a strong following even as questions bubble up about its potential sustainability, leading to short ideas and to an all out back and forth. I even broke out a life cycle for a high yield stock community on Seeking Alpha:
CBL & Associates ( CBL ) is decidedly somewhere between stage 4 and 5. The B and C-mall real estate operator has been a popular stock on Seeking Alpha; has cut its dividend and seen its stock drop meaningfully, and has seen a flurry of coverage on both the long and short (or at least bearish) side for months.
CBL data by YCharts
Michael Boyd has written presciently about several high yield companies in similar situations, including American Midstream ( AMID ) ( here ) and New Senior Investment ( SNR ) ( here ). He has been covering CBL regularly for about a year. This article looks at potential liquidation value for the company, not based on the balance sheet itself, but a practical sense of what current debt is and what the company might net in a liquidation. Per his analysis, a 12% cap rate = 0 equity value, and that's not so far from where CBL is priced now, with the market going in the wrong direction. It's an illustration of the impact of leverage, which can be very good when things turn higher and an anchor around a business's neck when the market climate decays.
Sentiment Check - I would characterize the commenter sentiment as more mixed, more of a stage 3 in the above table. Articles have turned more in favor of bearish viewpoints over the last 6 months, with something like two to one bearish to bullish analyses since the summer started.
The Most Obvious Short: Russian Steel Producers On Cycle Top by Russian Rocket Is it the most obvious short if you have to say it in the title? I don't know. But pitching a potential cyclical downturn in an area of the market that has less attention in the US at least makes sense. Russian Rocket has focused on Russia for their investment ideas so far, and they suggest Russian steel makers are priced at peak value despite facing headwinds in the cycle and from tariffs fall-out. They call out Evraz ( OTC:EVRZF ) as the most direct play on this theme, but also cited NLMK ( OTC:NISQY ), Severstal, MMK, and Mechel ( MTL ) as potential shorts. It's a quick and worthwhile read, and I like the effort put into this image:
Sentiment Check - Not a lot of Evraz sentiment or sentiment on any of these companies except MTL, which has attracted a mix of long and short ideas. Worth noting that in dollar terms, MTL is nowhere near highs.
Snap Has A Growing Problem (And Yes, We're Still Bearish) by Hedgeye Snap ( SNAP ) has been an easy target since it has come on the market, both for short sellers and for rivals like Facebook ( FB ). Hedgeye has been bearish all the way down, and they highlight an ongoing issue. This is a short video, but the analyst (Hesham Shabaan) points to decreased time per visit and limited usage of the discover section of the app as problems - Snap is still paying hosting costs without exposing users to ad inventory. He makes the comparison to Pandora ( P ), which is an interesting cross-industry look. Of course, Pandora just got a buyout offer, and while it never fulfilled its potential, the stock is trading now about where it bottomed after its IPO in 2012. Snap may head for the same end, but where is bottom?
Sentiment Check - We have more bottom-fishers than I expected - three authors have been bullish on SNAP since the start of Q3 - but there's a steady drumbeat of 'low-priced but not cheap or not worth buying' sentiment in our articles.
Why The Road For CBD-Infused Beverages May Be Longer And Harder Than Investors Anticipate by Altitrade Partners New Age Beverages Is Not A Cannabis Play Yet But Is Up On Hype A Month After A $1.28 Financing by Edward Vranic, CFA New Age Beverages Declines Have Just Begun by iWatchMarkets We've seen a pattern in the last 12-18 months where a bubble emerges in a sector of the market, and as a specific second-wave effect, other companies with no real connection to that bubble glom onto it, whether actively or passively, and stocks shoot up. The bitcoin/blockchain bubble was famous for it (hello OTCPK:LBCC ) and we have reached that phase with cannabis 2.0 (as compared to 1.0 in 2012-14, where this happened a lot on a more egregious scale).
DAVIDs Tea ( DTEA ) is my favorite example because the stock keeps popping up on my investing screens and I love tea but have never been able to justify an investment in the company. But New Age Beverages ( NBEV ) is the subject of three bearish articles this week.
The stock jumped on the potential of entering the cannabinoid/CBD beverage market, and/or the rumor that a beverage giant looking to partner with a smaller company might just buy NBEV. Jumped to the tune of nearly 400% in less than a week, before falling back about 50%. Which still has it more than 200% higher than where it was on September 14th.
This always seems like a fish in the barrel moment for market irrationality. Still, the articles review some things that may be helpful for future crazy moves. Vranic has the perspective of a former long, and his story recounts various times where the company hasn't quite executed on its aims, with limited profit growth being the main sticking point. Altitrade Partners adds perspective from their long time following Celsius Holdings ( CELH ), another micro-cap beverage maker that has struggled to scale to profitability. And iWatchMarkets has the benefit of writing after NBEV announced a $50M raise in at-the-market equity . It makes for an interesting study.
Sentiment Check - And to go further, comments seem fairly bullish and convinced the market is efficient in pricing NBEV much higher in a week. It's possible that a company would have value in the CBD beverage market - despite the concerns these authors raise - but seems unlikely that the value would be accurately recognized overnight, as has happened.
